items.title: Ashes of the Singularity 2 review: Some neat ideas undermined by a rubbish campaign and obtrusive generative AI

Expect to pay: £32.50/$39

Developer: Oxide Games

Publisher: Stardock

Reviewed On: AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Nvidia 2080 Super, 32 GB RAM, Windows 10.

Multiplayer? Yes

Steam Deck? Unsupported

Link: Official site 

Ashes of the Singularity 2 can't be faulted for scale. Much like its predecessor, the RTS sequel delivers on the promise of letting players control truly colossal armies. Rolling up huge globs of units and tossing them at your enemy lines in a giant, explosion-riddled mud fight is never subtle and only occasionally clever. But for any veteran RTS player, watching miles-long lines of armies clash is inevitably going to stir the soul.

Unfortunately, scale is also the sum of what Ashes of the Singularity 2 offers. As a sequel, it does little to build on the strengths of the original, while largely failing to address that first game's weaknesses. The campaign is terrible, the story borderline incomprehensible, and the whole experience is overshadowed by the spectre of generative AI.

You build your production buildings, your resource harvesters, your defensive structures, and that's more or less it.

items.title: 'Game dev isn't always straightforward': Overwatch's director responds to players upset about season 6's hero being a DPS

Hudson is the last hero to be released from the batch teased earlier this year during Overwatch's Spotlight , and after all this time I'm very excited to see what he has to offer. But not everyone shares this sentiment. 

There's a good chunk of players who are upset about Hudson, before they've even tried him out, simply because he's not a support hero, which was what Team 4 initially promised him to be. I've seen this discontent online and honestly ignored it, thinking it was either bots or people farming for attention because I cannot fathom why anyone is honestly upset about this. 

(Image credit: Blizzard Entertainment) I've been maining support in Overwatch for almost 10 years now, ever since open queue grinded me down and I accepted that no matter how much I liked DPS, I had to role fill if we wanted to win games. So, after all these years I love getting my hands on a new support hero, but after four new supports this year (including Sombra's transition to the role), I'm more than satisfied with the role's current diversity of heroes. 

But Team 4 is taking the criticism seriously, as Keller has addressed it directly. Aside from trying to convince players that shoehorning a hero into a role just because that was the plan 10 months ago isn't a great idea, he also explains how "game dev isn't always straightforward" and how the team needs "to adapt to create the best version of something".…

items.title: Intel hit with class action alleging it 'misled investors' – company's recent downturn due in part to how darn expensive PCs are right now
items.summary:
Hot on the heels of a monumental share price drop for the company, Intel now faces a class action lawsuit from its own shareholders. 

This is according to an alert from law firm Robbins LLP , which recently informed all investors. This suit alleges "Intel misled investors about demand for its products and the Company's future growth potential."

The class action can involve anyone who bought stock between July 23, 2026, and October 29, 2026, known as the "class period".

With the memory crisis in full effect, PC sales are down worldwide ( estimated to be 20% down in October ), but the lawsuit argues that the PC sales slowdown was "having a materially greater negative impact to Intel’s third quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Group results than defendants had disclosed to investors."

It also argues Intel's OEM and distribution partners were left with hardware they couldn't sell to consumers due to rising prices, and that positive impacts of Intel business coming from the AI boom were off "more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup."

(Image credit: Intel) The suit also alleges that Intel's reporting of its operations and ability to capitalise on the AI boom "were materially false and misleading when made, and such statements did not accurately reflect Intel’s then-present business and prospects."

With Robbins LLP informing investors of this class action lawsuit, it's possible more could join the claim, and we don't actually know how many are…
items.t: Intel hit with class action alleging it 'misled investors' – company's recent downturn due in part to how darn expensive PCs are right now

items.title: New Asus beta BIOS patches now include a fresh AMD feature to stop you thinking your PC's b0rked
items.summary:
Memory training is boring stuff. Your PC will spend an age running through it when you first boot your PC, or you swap in some new RAM sticks (lucky you), or you make a change which has anything to do with memory in your BIOS. Or just because your PC decides it might fancy doing it again. But a new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta BIOS update, first from Asus (via Uniko's Hardware ), has made this whole process a lot more exciting.

Well, going from not at all exciting to something is always going to feel like a bigger deal, but I don't necessarily want to oversell it. Though when you're waiting for memory training to complete it's real nice to at least have a readout to indicate that it is progressing and your PC hasn't just hung.

This is the issue with memory training on PCs in the past. It was pretty damned opaque, in that you'd start up your PC and it would do… nothing. The fans would spin up, and the lights would light, but you'd have no readout on your monitor, and the debug screen on your motherboard would just have a static figure. Mine would be stuck on '15' for an age. 

Obviously you could just go looking up the error code and it would inform you that your system was just having a good long think about its system memory, but if you didn't know that could be a thing, it can feel like your rig is bricked.

The new AGESA 1.3.0.1F beta patches are out now, first from Asus, but you can bet other motherboard vendors will be following suit soon enough. This latest version of the AGESA BIOS brings with it AMD's new memory training function, which shows on the motherboard's debug…
items.t: New Asus beta BIOS patches now include a fresh AMD feature to stop you thinking your PC's b0rked

items.title: Fable Reveals First Look At Bowerstone's New Map, And It's Huge
items.summary:
Over the weekend, Xbox released a digital magazine featuring details on upcoming games. One of the games featured heavily is the long-awaited Fable revival, set to launch next February after numerous delays . 

In a six-page spread, the magazine gives us a bunch of new details about Fable, including some returning features and new quests. However, the big pull here is that it finally reveals the full scope of the capital city, Bowerstone, showing us exactly how it will look 16 years after we last saw it in Fable 3.

As we can see on the map, Bowerstone will be split into three districts in the new Fable. Those districts are:

Butterfield Market: The centre of commerce in Bowerstone. Shops and stalls can be found here, and all can be purchased by the player. Copperbottom: Home of the working class. Placed physically lower on the map, Copperbottom gets less sunlight and has become a hotbed of criminal activity. Reminds me somewhat of Bowerstone Industrial in Fable 3. Bowerminster: Where you'll find the nobility, including the residents of Fairfax Castle — the one you could buy at the end of Fable 2. On top of this, familiar landmarks can be found in these districts:

Fairfax Castle (returning from Fable 2, and sort of Fable 3) The Old Clock Tower (returning from Fable 2 and 3) The Heroes' Guild (returning from the first Fable) From this, we can see that Playground Games has mashed all the different Bowerstones in the original Fable trilogy together. We have the whimsy of the first game with the Heroes' Guild being attached to the city, the budding aristocracy of the second…

items.title: Anthony Mackie Insists He Didn't Spoil Avengers: Doomsday by Revealing an Unannounced Character

Marvel star Anthony Mackie has insisted he did not drop a big Avengers: Doomsday spoiler last week, when he appeared to reveal an unannounced character.

In an interview with Entertainment Tonight , Mackie said he had enjoyed filming Marvel's upcoming mega blockbuster as it had given him a chance to "just catch up with everybody." Specifically, Mackie mentioned singled out his downtime with Shang-Chi star Simu Liu and VisionQuest actor Paul Bettany as particular highlights. 

As Marvel fans will know, Bettany's character Vision is yet to be confirmed as appearing in Doomsday — something that many pointed out in response to Mackie's statement. So, in other words, why was Bettany around to hang out with?

Now, however, Mackie has appeared on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon to set the record straight — and insist that Avengers' production simply gave him the chance to visit Bettany on the separate VisionQuest production that was going on next door.

"Paul Bettany is my man, my homie, we hang out all the time," Mackie began. "He was shooting VisionQuest next door to where we were shooting Avengers. So, me being me, I steal a golf cart and pull up. I'm a pull-upper.

"So I didn't say he was in Doomsday, I said he was next door shooting his show. Just like Tom Holland was next door shooting Spider-Man.

"He was next door!" Mackie concluded. "He wasn't in the movie... I guess?"

Somewhat ironically, Mackie's claim is backed up by an actual Marvel set leak from last year , where an Instagram user somehow managed to get into the production area at the U.K.'s Leavesdon…

items.title: WoW: Forever's continued to wrestle with dungeons, as Blizzard admits it briefly 'missed the mark' on hotfixes over the weekend
items.summary:
World of Warcraft: Forever 's been pretty great. At this point, I have around 150 hours played, a terrible posture problem, and a level 47 warrior I just barely avoided doing a 2 am Zul'Farrak run with yesterday. Speaking of, there has been a point of contention: Dungeons. 

My position on the debate is fairly neutral —I think you could maybe bump up the mob XP by around 10% as a compromise—but overall I think they're fine. The new ones are bangers, and I get a huge bunch of XP from doing them at least once. Blizzard's recent choices, however, did have me scratching my head over the weekend.

For a short time, via a hotfix , enemies in dungeons wouldn't give experience points to anyone in the group if they were trivial (that is, greyed out) to at least one party member. On paper, this sounds incredibly reasonable. WoW has suffered from a plague of dungeon boosters (that is, people selling runs of dungeons to let folks AFK through their levelling journey) particularly in Classic. 

But the moment you take a second to stare at how Classic dungeons are designed, you start to see the cracks form. Uldaman, for instance, has a level range of 41-51 in my dungeon finder. Maraudon, 46-55. Then there's the issue of the Scarlet Monastery, whose entire gauntlet runs from level 30 to 44 and is often done in one big sweep by groups.

items.title: The latest SteamOS update improves support on Nvidia-powered PCs: makes swapping your rig to the OS less painful

The preview version of SteamOS 3.10.0 has just dropped, and with it comes better support for AMD and Nvidia hardware, and it's now based on Linux kernel 7.3. 

For AMD graphics, the latest SteamOS update adds support for HDMI 2.1 VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), FRL(Fixed Rate Link), and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode). This should all contribute to a smoother gaming experience with higher bandwidth video and less input lag. 

As for Nvidia graphics, it has reportedly received increased stability and performance, alongside support for Mesh Shaders on Turing and newer architectures. The latest SteamOS updates also fixed rendering corruption issues in Shadow of the Tomb Raider and The Surge 2. 

Then, of course, SteamOS now uses the Linux 7.3 kernel (which launched last month). 

Those are the big updates from SteamOS 3.10.0, but there are also a handful of fixes and changes. Game Mode has had the following changes:

VisionQuest creator Terry Matalas has explained why Agatha Harkness failed to appear on screen during the series — despite her presence being felt. 

Before its launch, VisionQuest was described as the concluding chapter of the WandaVision trilogy (which began with WandaVision, and continued with Agatha All Along as its sandwich filling) — so there was some expectation that the sorceress from both series might reappear. But, alas, she did not — and Matalas has now explained why.

Warning: Spoilers for VisionQuest follow... 

The finale of VisionQuest sees the return of Joe Locke's Billy Maximoff from Agatha All Along, as he reunites with Tommy Maximoff and his synthezoid sort-of father Vision. This picks up directly from WandaVision's final scene, where Billy sets off to go find his brother aided by a ghostly Harkness, who has now left her physical body behind. 

While Agatha does not appear on screen in VisionQuest, Billy still talks briefly with her. Tommy even realizes that Billy is doing so, and makes a comment about his brother having an invisible friend — as Harkness does not appear to him (or the audience). 

While it would have been great to see her physically (or spectrally) again, the dialogue is still a neat way of acknowledging her presence and confirming she's still helping Billy. But why not have Kathryn Hahn back for a cameo?

items.title: AI Chat App Character.ai is Attempting to Stave Off Bankruptcy, And Has a $20 Million Offer From Disney
items.summary:
Character.ai went live in 2022, alongside many other AI apps like ChatGPT, forever changing the online landscape (for the worse, many would argue). 

While it never became a household name, like ChatGPT, Grok, or Gemini, Character.ai found its place in online fandom spaces. This is because the app allows users to make their own AI companions and share them with others, and this was quickly used to make copyrighted characters from film, television, video games, and more. 

It is no surprise, then, that the service ran into many legal and ethical issues. Some copyright holders would do what they could to have their characters removed from the service, and moderators would struggle to remove bots based on real people. More seriously, questions were raised about the safety measures in place to protect users, as at least two minors were found to have used Character.ai extensively before they died by suicide. This resulted in two lawsuits, one of which has since been settled . 

Throughout all of this, Character.ai has been struggling to turn its sizeable user base into profit. Despite several attempts to turn this around — rolling out new features, ads, and testing out subscription fees — Character.ai has been unsuccessful and has now filed for bankruptcy. 

In October, Disney came to the company's aid, paying $60 million to grab 66 of Character.ai's employees (as per Business Insider ). It has further proposed paying $20 million to acquire some of Character.ai's tech, leading to speculation that Disney is looking to enter the AI chatbot space, perhaps with its own copyrighted…

As the car pulled a corner, a whistle cried out from a nearby rooftop. With that, a couple of bikes shot down alleyways, pedalling fast to catch up before pulling up either side of the car to escort it on its patrol through the neighbourhood. items.title: Influential Warhammer miniature designer Aly Morrison has died
items.summary:
Miniature designer and artist Aly Morrison has died, as confirmed by Trish Carden Miniatures and Design on Facebook . Carden, Morrison's ex-wife and former partner in Marauder Miniatures, posted that, "Mharaid and I are heartbroken to announce the passing of Aly Morrison, a very much loved father, veteran wargames miniatures designer and friend to many around the tabletop and the world. Aly passed unexpectedly but peacefully this Wednesday, and will be sorely missed."

Aly Morrison began sculpting for Citadel in 1983 as a freelancer before joining the studio full-time in 1986. He and Trish were then made stewards of Games Workshop's imprint Marauder Miniatures in 1988, where they had free reign to create quirky and characterful figures like the mohawked dwarf trollslayers and the giant with a whaler's beard and a booze barrel strapped to his waist that became archetypal parts of Warhammer.

Morrison also crafted the first miniatures for Blood Bowl players and drew the tokens to represent them in the board game's first edition. During his time at Games Workshop every faction from dark elves to space marines eventually benefited from his touch.

He's also well-regarded as a painter, and his reliance on a dark wash with a hint of purple in it jokingly known as "Aly's Brown Liquid" was legendary. He continued working on the recipe over the years, with a recent iteration described on his blog in 2020 if you want to whip some up yourself.

It's no secret that the Covid-19 pandemic saw a lot of people using videogames to stave off lockdown blues, and the Jackbox Party Pack games were especially well-suited for the role: easy-to-understand party fare that's optionally family-friendly and easy to play over a video call. PC Gamer said as much back in March 2020.

In a recent interview with PC Gamer associate editor Ted Litchfield, Jackbox Games CEO Mike Bilder said that the pandemic proved transformative for the developer. 

"The industry at large obviously saw a lot of success at that time, but we did as well, and we went from a gamer name to a household name," he said, noting it was an "unfortunate period of time for the world, but for the gaming industry, a good one, and for Jackbox, a good one as well."

"That was kind of a leveling up for Jackbox as a company," said Bilder. "Suddenly office workers are doing happy hours and families over weekends are connecting over a game of Whiplash or something because it's what you did when you were locked down. People realized how easy it was to just share the screen over a Zoom call and everyone's playing."

It surprised employees at the studio to see how popular the games had become. 

Chief marketing officer Brooke Hofer recalled a scene in the 2022 Knives Out sequel Glass Onion, where characters could be seen playing Quiplash over a Zoom call: "I remember when we all saw that in the studio, and we're like, 'Whoa,' you know. But that was so many people's experience at that time, and it was cool how that was captured in pop culture in various ways."

items.title: Slay the Spire 2 has a new character in testing, and she's really quite busted
items.summary:
Slay the Spire 2 has a new character—notably, a new character in testing —and as the patch notes themselves point out , that testing will very much be needed: "We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch."

I decided to hop into the beta branch myself and take her for a whirl, and—yeah, those changes'll have to come. The Fool's central mechanic is her bow and arrow—she can fire an arrow/shoot card to deal damage equal to the card's base damage plus her aim. So if a shoot card deals 15 damage and she has six aim stocked, she'll deal 21. 

This is a little busted, because by default, the Fool has 6 aim already put in her bank. Her non-strike starter card, Foolish Shot, already deals a hefty 15 damage for just one energy. With aim, the first time she uses it, it deals a whopping 21 damage, which is a heck of a damage output for the Fool's first round of combat.

The saving grace here is that when a card that fires an arrow is used, that arrow becomes lodged in a target, who gains the Impale status. You can't play any more arrow-based cards until you either Dislodge (another game term, hence the proper nounage) an arrow with a card that dislodges, or until you have more than one arrow.

In my runs, I wasn't able to figure out the latter. But I really didn't need to, because I was one-shotting bosses the whole way up the spire. One card in particular, Repeat Shot, seems borderline broken. While it is a rare, it shoots a target for 20 damage (when upgraded) X times, plus your current aim.

items.title: Xbox at 25: My Memories From Across Xbox’s Entire (and Quite Incredible) History
items.summary:
The first day of my career was October 1, 2002. I’d been lucky enough to get hired by Official Xbox Magazine. The fledgling Xbox console was not quite a year old, and when I got settled in on the staff, it quickly became clear that Xbox was really about one thing above all else: Halo. I remember being surprised in my first days on the job by what would happen every single day, like clockwork, at 5pm: consoles and TVs would get turned on, Halo would get fired up, and we’d all play a round or two of Capture the Flag on Blood Gulch before we all went home. Fun and friendly banter ensued. Halo was baked into the Xbox’s DNA from the very start.

It is one of my very first of many thousands of great Xbox memories. I’ve been lucky enough to have a front-row seat for most of the Xbox’s 25 years, covering the high highs and low lows of Microsoft’s pivot into the living room. It’s been quite a ride since November 15, 2001, and I wanted to mark the occasion by sharing some of my biggest memories with you. And, like everything else with Xbox, it started with Halo.

Thank goodness for Combat Evolved, in fact, because most of the rest of that first year of Xbox history was pretty bleak. Lots of C++ spaghetti was thrown at the wall, and most of it didn’t stick. Oh, don’t get me wrong – there were moments! Steel Battalion, Capcom’s batshit-insane mech vertical tank simulator that cost $200 and came with its own custom 40-button controller and foot pedals was quite simply amazing as both a game and piece of hardware and would never get made today. You are at, I don't know, some sort of family dining experience. There is a stage. On the stage, there is a magician. You are called up, and made to select a card from a deck of 52. "Don't show me, don't show me", exclaims the sorcerer. There is a dramatic pause, and then he reveals—from his own pocket—your card. Polite applause . 

He keeps going: from his other pocket, your wallet. From his shirt, your wedding ring. Under his hat, your pet hamster, clutching in its teeth a love letter you wrote to your wife when you were first dating. The magician removes his mask—he is you, and you are your wife. Also, throughout this process, someone has given you a backpack and keeps adding exotic hammers to it.

This is what playing Queen's Domain feels like.

items.title: This RTS inspired by Star Wars: Empire at War promises colossal space encounters and planetary battles with 'hundreds of thousands of units'
items.summary:
I could claim that I love real-time strategy games for their fast-paced decision-making. But what I truly love is building massive armies and wreaking havoc on an apocalyptic scale. So when I saw the trailer for Horu (via RPS ), an in-development RTS that promises "hundreds of thousands of units" on screen, it went on the wishlist faster than you can say 'Zerg Rush'.

Horu is an upcoming strategy game inspired by Total War and Star Wars: Empire at War , aiming to blend the colossal battles of the former with the galaxy-scale strategy of the latter. It challenges players to establish their own interstellar empire, building vast space fleets and huge land armies to assume ultimate dominion of the cosmos.

While it's the spectacle of Horu that caught my attention, with clouds of spaceships trading laser fire and oceans of little men getting obliterated by artillery, there are a couple of more specific ideas and mechanics that also sound deeply exciting. Unlike the games that inspired it, Horu aspires to be fully real-time, with battles playing out simultaneously across the solar system. This includes both land and space battles, letting you do things like punch your dropships through an enemy's orbital fleet to land an army on the surface while the battle in space rages on.

This sounds rad, but also like it might be challenging to keep track of. Thankfully, Horu promises a few mechanics to keep the scale manageable. This includes a "drop zone system" that lets you assign a drop zone on a planet and queue up a set of orders, which the assigned army will then carry out…

items.title: The Sunday Papers
items.summary:
While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?
items.t: The Sunday Papers

items.title: Former survival MMO Dune: Awakening can now be played 'without requiring an Internet connection at any point' as its much requested offline mode arrives
items.summary:
At long last, the transfer of power is complete. Dune: Awakening , Funcom's ambitious survival MMO based on the classic sci-fi novel, has completed is pivot away from massive multiplayer, and can now be played fully offline.

The offline function arrived in an otherwise unremarkable patch that mainly fixes specific bugs and technical issues. "It's now possible to play the game in single-player mode without requiring an internet connection at any point, including creating and deleting single-player characters.," Funcom revealed in a Steam post. 

Dune: Awakening has been gradually drifting away from being a purely multiplayer experience for some time. In April, Funcom made its PvP element, like the Deep Desert and shipwreck exploration, fully optional . A fully fledged single-player mode arrived in September, including a dramatic rework of several major endgame systems—like its dynamic political "Landsraad" system' to make them work in solo play. At that point, single-player still required an Internet connection. Now though, that's no longer the case.

To be clear, Dune: Awakening can still be played with all its multiplayer and PvP trappings, now including a "Go Online" button for exactly that purpose. Nonetheless, it's been a fascinating shift in direction, one that, alongside games like Marathon , embodies a broader apparent trend away from large-scale. competitive multiplayer experiences toward smaller, cooperative communities. Whether with friends or alone, players increasingly want to be able to live in their own worlds, unbothered by the wider, more tumultuous…

items.title: Chronicles: Medieval developer declared bankruptcy on the day it announced it was in trouble, but development will continue after a $5 million reprieve from Coffee Stain
items.summary:
In late October, Chronicles: Medieval developer Raw Power Games announced that it was in trouble . Funding for its ambitious, historical sandbox strategy had suddenly been pulled, and as a result the studio was at "real risk of closing". But it turns out the situation was even more dire than the announcement suggested, as Raw Power Games declared bankruptcy on the same day.

Despite this, development of Chronicles: Medieval will continue with at least some of its original creators involved, after Satisfactory owners Coffee Stain Group swooped in to purchase the assets and IP.

In a press release , Coffee Stain said that it submitted the winning bid in Raw Power's sale process following the company's bankruptcy, paying 36.75 million Danish Krone (around $5.42 million) for Chronicles: Medieval's intellectual property.

Rather than acquire the assets directly, however, Coffee Stain will transfer them directly to a "newly established company" that is owned 75% by Coffee Stain, and 25% by "a small group of key members of the game's original development team." Alongside paying full purchase price for Chronicles: Medieval's assets, Coffee Stain will also fund the continued development of the game.

In a statement, Coffee Stain CEO Anton Westbergh said that "Chronicles: Medieval made a strong impression at its reveal at Summer Game Fest last year. We're happy to step in and help bring it to players after the recent developments in Copenhagen." Moira Brown gets a bad rap. Fallout 3's most chipper NPC, the Minnesotan menace is an inventor who sends you out on fact-finding missions to investigate the many dangers of the Wasteland. That means she puts you in harm's way quite a lot, which many players hate her for. Others just hate her voice.

I think her positive outlook makes a refreshing change of pace from, you know, everything else going on in Fallout 3. Plus she gives you an armored Vault suit just for starting her questline, and the Wasteland Survival Guide she writes with your help goes on to be a useful item in both New Vegas and Fallout 4. 

What I'm saying is, there are plenty of videogame questgivers much more annoying than Moira Brown. All of the ones below, for starters. And if you disagree, you're a big meanie.

Rockstar loves to make us sit through cutscenes where our protagonist agrees to help out some of the most annoying people alive. Zero isn't alone—in GTA: San Andreas, he's got wannabe MC/janitor OG Loc for competition—but he is the winner for absolute worst.

items.title: Planeswalker, Netflix's Magic: The Gathering animated series, will have a different art style for each plane
items.summary:
Netflix's Magic: The Gathering series was initially announced in 2019 with the MCU's Russo Brothers at the helm, though they left a couple of years later thanks to the all-purpose "creative differences". That was all we heard until 2024 until Brandon Routh, who had been cast as planeswalker Gideon Jura, casually mentioned in an unrelated interview that the project had been binned.

Netflix announced soon after that actually the animated series was a go, now with Terry Matalas of Star Trek: Picard and the 12 Monkeys TV series as its head showrunner, with a teaser image showing pyromancer Chandra and leonin Ajani Goldmane silhouetted against a red sky.

Now, a mere seven years after the first reveal, there's a "sneak peek" trailer with a bunch of excited Wizards of the Coast staff, art labeled "early development", and a few seconds of Ajani and Chandra doing their stuff. 

The most intriguing part is when, over a montage of 3D props including a car that looks like an art deco Batmobile from New Capenna, executive producer and supervising director Patrick Osborne says, "All the planes exist in their own pocket universe. That comes with culture, design language, architecture, and we're even making the film-making style different depending on where it is."

That's a good idea. An animated series with different art styles for each plane the characters travel to would be a great way of representing Magic, a card game where every artist gets to put their own spin on how things look. items.title: WoW: Forever dungeon mobs no longer give EXP if they're trivial for anyone in the party
items.summary:
It's been something of a rollercoaster watching Blizzard tweak the experience rewards players can expect from dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever. They've always been a reliable way to get oodles of experience and fat loots, but in Forever, the goal has seemingly been to ensure they're more of a supplement to regular questing and exploration.

Initially, mob experience values were nerfed pretty hard to compensate for a boost in quest experience, meaning that you'd get diminishing returns for spamming one dungeon over and over. Later, dungeon enemy experience was buffed by a lot, but not back to its pre-nerf value. 

In a hotfix released yesterday , dungeon experience was tweaked yet again: "Killing enemies in dungeons now awards zero experience to all party members if the level of the enemy is trivial to the level of one or more of the party members," the note reads.

A mob is considered trivial in World of Warcraft when it's a significantly lower level than you (the exact threshold changes based on your level)—you'll know an enemy is trivial to your character when its level is displayed in a gray font.

This change seems aimed at higher-level players boosting their friends or a group of paying customers through instances, potentially offsetting the experience nerfs by clearing the dungeon and its quests much faster.

items.title: Is the game funny, or just the players? Jackbox CEO says they get 'a lot of false positives' with a staff of comedy writers
items.summary:
Social improv games like those in Jackbox 's Party Packs can have vastly different vibes depending on who you're playing with. Meemaw isn't likely to appreciate the phrase "glup shitto" the way your PC gaming friends will, and those sorts of high-variance dynamics are something Jackbox Games has to stay acutely aware of, according to CEO Mike Bilder. 

"I mean we do a ton [of testing] internally, but then as games get greenlit, we'll bring in external groups," Bilder told PC Gamer associate editor Ted Litchfield in a recent interview. "We want to make sure that we're not just local-biased with our own opinions on things. We want to make sure these games are playing well."

Something that makes it especially hard to tell whether a game is funny or they're just having a good session is the fact that they work with comedy writers—people who can make a boring game seem funny just by cracking jokes while they play.

"We get a lot of false positives because we have such funny people here that work in the office, and they make games shine," said Bilder. "No matter what the concept is, you're gonna laugh, or the way they're hosting or emceeing the game, the pitch is hilarious, and it's like, can the game do that? Or is it just [studio creative director Arnie Niekamp]? Arnie's funny … a lot of times it is just Arnie."

In the same interview, Bilder also commented on generative AI . "The people are what make this product," he said. "The comedy, the writing, and the art, all that is done by people, and we have no intention of changing that."
items.t: Is the game funny, or just the players? Jackbox CEO says they get 'a lot of false positives' with a staff of comedy writers

items.title: Do you like mob tagging in oldschool MMOs, or are you done with fighting for quest credit?
items.summary:
Terminally Online 

(Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.

I've been having a pleasant time with WoW: Forever (and by that, I mean it has consumed nearly every waking moment of my life). One thing, however, has been made pretty clear: Mob tagging, that is, only giving kill credit to the first player (or group) to damage a mob, is divisive. 

One side of the fence—my side, I'm afraid—does see mob tagging as a necessary evil in an MMO that's trying to drive social interaction. Videogames, particularly ones that are incentivising you to group up, are kind of meant to be a pain in the butt sometimes; if you've got a "kill 20" quest and there another person there, the fact you might get in each other's way if you don't group up, and have a jollier time if you do, is a net good.

I have more complicated thoughts on item drop quests being bad in a group, sure. And I'd like it if Blizzard's layering technology was a little more merciful. But, overall, I'm all for it. Nearly every single person I've thrown an invite to has grouped up with me, and I've even (gasp) had conversations with strangers. Pleasant ones!

Some of them are even on my friends list now, and it is, I think, a point in my favour that I would have largely ignored every single person I am now regularly chatting to if mob tagging…

Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager .

What's the fastest you've ever fallen in love with a game? I think I have a new record: about 0.3 seconds into CultGame , when launching it from Steam spawned not a regular game window, but a command prompt instance. Perfection. Chef's kiss. No notes.

Like the Bay 12 games (Dwarf Fortress and especially Liberal Crime Squad ) it clearly takes inspiration from, CultGame is gloriously text-based. Its art is ASCII, its options selected by tippy-tapping the numpad, its maps are carpets of symbols: lurid at signs and hashes as far as the eye can see.

It's a management game, first and foremost. Once you have generated a world and a history for it, you choose the precise nature of cult leader you wish to be: Defector Cleric, Occult Scholar, Con Artist, or Lunatic, and off you go. I was Gideon Faircloth, the fallen cleric, and my object of reverence was a 'World's Best Grandpa' Cup whose domains were blood and fire. 

CultGame lets you rewrite basically everything, including the deity type you follow; it does not protest, I learnt, when you write some absolute nonsense in there. I learnt this lesson again when the game asked me to choose a creed for my nascent faith and I wrote "Opinions are not those of my…

items.title: Dishonored 2 director Harvey Smith wants to honour sacred imsim texts while finding news ways to surprise fans: 'That's the two wolves inside me'
items.summary:
Harvey Smith remembers the 10 months he spent as quality assurance lead on System Shock as a "brush with greatness".

"I had loved Ultima Underworld, and then I got to work with the very people that were rolling off of Underworld onto this new cyberpunk game," he says. "Looking Glass fought like cats and dogs, but man, they were passionate about what they were doing. And this was a mission for them."

(Image credit: Nightdive) Afterwards, when Smith joined System Shock producer Warren Spector at Ion Storm Austin, "we just applied that same hunger to Deus Ex ," he says. "And then when I got together with Raphaël Colantonio, we were like, 'Why just live a normal life? Why fucking punch in and sit at a desk and run some numbers? We're just dying to do this, right?' And so we made Dishonored ."

It's a simplified take on the story—one that skips the wilderness years spent fighting for funding before Arkane partnered with Bethesda. But the stubborn and single-minded outlook Smith describes is crucial to explaining his career in immersive sims. If he had been more sensible—less determined to funnel his days into spiritually satisfying work in the genre that first lit his creative fire—Arkane would never have made Dishonored at all.

"When Arkane was independent, very often people would come in and they would try to get us to work on some game that was not in our wheelhouse," he says. "People would say, 'You're going to go under by turning your nose up at doing this DLC for this third-person action shooter, this is money.' And we'd be like, 'Yeah, but we don't like those. We…

items.title: How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games
items.summary:
Much like the H.P. Lovecraft novella it alternately riffs on and skewers, Penguin Colony takes you to an ancient alien city of crabby cuboid geometry and helical designs – comparable at a glance to Lovecraft's "terraces of every sort of provocative disproportion", but here given strangely everyday, anachronistic-seeming labels, such as "Downtown". Later, you're shown flashes of footage of the streets of Melbourne in Australia - developer Origame Digital's base of operations, and a city built on stolen Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung and Bunurong Boon Wurrung land.

When I first set foot in Downtown, in the unassuming body of a Rockhopper penguin, I thought the broad idea was to satirically redefine modern settlements built by European colonisers as Lovecraftian relics, intrusions from the cosmic beyond. This irony seems most pointed in sections where you steer a group of Māori characters, journeying south to prevent an expedition of German and British Nazi occultists from resurrecting a surviving elder being they call the "one true Aryan king". Playing as one of the Māori voyagers, you witness the cyclopean city as a realm of spectral high rises and square windows, rearing out of a swamp of blood and bone.
items.t: How Origame Digital are channelling and defacing Lovecraft over a trilogy of "inherently indigenous" anti-fascist games

items.title: Horu is a sci-fi 4X RTS inspired by Star Wars: Empire at War in which spaceships are spellcasters who can summon black holes

Clicking a random link this morning, I was dazzled by the glare of a thousand laser batteries firing simultaneously. My ears trembled beneath the trundle of a million caterpillar tracks. Balls of ice, bolts of lightning, shipments of rare alloys, and cascades of drop pods went screaming down my nerves and detonated in my frontal cortex, painting starlanes across the inside of my skull. "Oh god, they've finally found us!" I yelled, hiding beneath my desk. "I for one welcome our new galactic overlords!"

But then I realised that I wasn't looking at a live newsfeed, but merely the Steam page for Horu, a real-time 4X strategy game in which you can "command hundreds of thousands of units across land and space", in the summary of developer David "GlassBeaver" Nadaski. There's also a magic system, this being "the spice that makes your enemy's defeat bitter", which is a very genteel way to characterise glaciating a tank formation or conjuring a miniature blackhole.
